nodes.description: Axiom Gamma is a completely open source 4K filmmaking camera. Its open and modular design enables customization and advanced experimentation in artistic, scientific and industrial applications. In its basic configuration, the camera uses a CMV12000 image sensor which supports up to 12MP (4096x3072 pixels) and offers image capture at speeds of up to 300fps. The image sensor's APS-like optical format makes it compatible with a variety of APS-C lenses and apertures created for professional photography and filmmaking. Images are processed with interchangeable modules with programmable logic (FPGA) which allow full customization of the image acquisition process and further processing. The camera is wrapped in a custom-designed enclosure compatible with a variety of tripods, rigs and sound and lighting accessories that are widely used in the filmmaking industry.

This component integrates all the image processing modules installed on the camera. It supplies power to all of the modules and break-routes a JTAG chain which can be used for configuring all the modules with a single JTAG programmer. The backplane PCB features a daisy-chain connection topology in which a set of output data lanes from one module is provided to the corresponding inputs of another module. This allows each module to control the data passing between modules by simply re-routing the data from input/output lanes.

The Sensor Board includes a mount for the CMV12000 image sensor. It break-routes the sensor interface into a set of board-to-board connectors that allow the sensor to be installed on the Preprocessing Module with a set of flex cables that compensate vibrations. The board's shape also allows for heat dissipation from the image sensor body, minimizing thermal noise.

The Central Processing Module is responsible for advanced video operations. It is based on an AMD (formerly Xilinx) ZYNQ SoC which combines ARM-based processor with programmable logic. The board also features a discrete RAM IC for the CPU and an additional slot for DDR3 SO-DIMM memory for the FPGA part. The Zynq SoC runs Linux, enabling control over the camera unit. The board includes a Gigabit Ethernet Interface that can be used for remote access and commissioning of the camera.

This board provides power to the Backplane rear connector and routes the data lanes going out from the Backplane into a board-to-board connector which lets you connect an optional Low Speed IO expansion module.

The Preprocessing Module is responsible for low-level image acquisition from the CMV12000 Sensor Board. It includes an AMD (formerly Xilinx) Kintex-7 FPGA which interfaces directly with LVDS high speed lanes exposed from the CM12000 image sensor. The FPGA runs a RISC-V soft core responsible for lane training to enable in-sync image data acquisition. The FPGA on the Preprocessing Module allows for performing low-level operations, e.g. image processing, noise reduction, black/white balancing, cropping and/or scaling. The image processing pipeline depends on the bitstream configuration. The Preprocessing Kintex-7 FPGA passes the video data captured from the CM12000 signal to the camera backplane for further processing. The image acquisition and preprocessing system synthesized in the Kintex-7 FPGA can also make use of the on-board SO-DIMM DDR3 slot that supports off-the-shelf memory modules.

The Lotus Elise chassis-based Tesla Roadster, the first serial production, all-electric car to use lithium-ion battery cells, debuted in 2008, offering unprecedented travel range. The open source release of some of the assets constituting the hardware and software of the Roadster, including the Vehicle Management System, the Vehicle Display System and the Battery Management System, opened the possibility of employing tools such as Renode and the hardware library to visualize, analyze and simulate the released components.

The Battery Management Board in the Tesla Roadster is responsible for monitoring and managing the performance of the lithium-ion battery cells that power the vehicle. It plays a pivotal role in maintaining the balance and health of the battery pack, which is essential for the vehicle's overall efficiency and safety. It's managed by the Vehicle Management System.

nodes.category: Boards/Tesla Roadster Vehicle Display System board
nodes.description: The Tesla Roadster Vehicle Display System Board is a crucial component of the vehicle's user interface, responsible for managing the digital displays and providing drivers with vital information and controls. The VDS is designed to drive the vehicle's digital dashboard and infotainment displays, delivering real-time data, navigation, multimedia, and vehicle controls to the driver and passengers. It's managed by the Vehicle Management System.

The Vehicle Management System (VMS) in the Tesla Roadster is a sophisticated system designed to monitor, control, and optimize the vehicle's performance and safety. It manages and communicates with the Battery Management System (BMS) for managing the lithium-ion battery pack, the Power Electronics Module (PEM) for controlling power flow between the battery and motor, the Vehicle Display System (VDS) for managing the digital displays, and the Motor Control System for torque and speed management. Additionally, the VMS provides telemetry and diagnostics for real-time data and remote support, a user interface for driver interaction, and safety systems for collision detection and airbag deployment. The VMS firmware is supported in the Renode simulation framework.

nodes.description:
The AD2S1210 is a complete 10-bit to 16-bit resolution tracking
resolver-to-digital converter, integrating an on-board programmable
sinusoidal oscillator that provides sine wave excitation for
resolvers.

The AD2S1210 allows the user to read the angular position or the
angular velocity data directly from the parallel outputs or through
the serial interface.

The mode of operation of the communication channel (parallel or serial) is
selected by the A0 and A1 input pins. In normal mode, data is latched by
toggling the SAMPLE line and can then be read directly. In configuration mode,
data is read or written using a register access scheme (address byte with
read/write flag and data byte).

  A1  A0  Result
   0   0  Normal mode - position output
   0   1  Normal mode - velocity output
   1   0  Reserved
   1   1  Configuration mode

In normal mode, the resolution of the digital output is selected using
the RES0 and RES1 input pins. In configuration mode, the resolution is
selected by setting the RES0 and RES1 bits in the control register.

RES1  RES0  Resolution (Bits)
   0     0  10
   0     1  12
   1     0  14
   1     1  16

Note on SPI connections: The CS line on the AD2S1210 should hard-wired to
logic low and the WR/FSYNC line on the AD2S1210 should be connected to the
SPI CSn output of the SPI controller.
